Notes

Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

This family of Neural Networks are specifically designed to operator on images with channels.

Hence, the input space X= Rci​×hi​×wi​, where i subscript here will stand for input image related attributes.

The output space will depend on the tasks, some common ones being covered in the last section.

The core novelty in this chapter is the convolution layer, which takes in a channeled image and outputs another channeled image, i.e. X= Rci​×hi​×wi​ and Y =Rco​×ho​×wo​ where the o subscript stands for output attributes.

The dual of that is the Transposed convolution Layer which is actually the adjoint operator of the original conv2D operation.

1. Building Blocks of core CNN

This section deals with convolution layer and its variants. In short, the convolution layer family is an image-to-image type of layer. Hence, X= Rci​×hi​×wi​ and Y =Rco​×ho​×wo​.

1.1 Base Operations in CNN

The two basic operations in CNN are: cross-correlation and transposed convolution

Definition 1.1 [Cross-Correlation; Transposed Convolution]

1. [Cross Correlation]
Given an image X∈Rh×w and a kernel K∈Rhk​×wk​, the cross-correlation operation, Y=K⋆X :

​Y∈Rho​×wo​, where ho​=hi​−hk​+1,wo​=wi​−wk​+1Yi,j​=m,n=0∑hk​−1,wk​−1​Km,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​​​i=0,1,⋯ho​−1j=0,1,⋯wo​−1​​

In Signal Processing terminology, this is valid mode cross-correlation.

Cross-correlation may be visualized as follows:

2. [Transposed Convolution]
Given a kernel K∈Rhk​×wk​ and G∈Rho​×wo​, the transposed convolution Z=K⋆TG is defined as full mode convolution of G with K:

​Z∈Rh×w,h=ho​+hk​−1,w=wo​+wk​−1Zi,j​=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,nrot180​⋅Gi−m,j−npad​i=0,1,⋯h−1,j=0,1,⋯w−1where Km,nrot180​=Khk​−1−m,wk​−1−n​≡rot180(K)Gi,jpad​={Gi,j​,0,​0≤i≤hk​−1,0≤j≤wk​−1otherwise​≡pad(G;hk​−1,wk​−1)∴Z=rot180(K)⋆pad(G;hk​−1,wk​−1)​

where Gpad denotes G zero-padded to all indices (i.e. Gp,qpad​=0 whenever (p,q) falls outside G’s domain).

In Signal Processing terminology, this is exactly full mode convolution — equivalently, pad G with hk​−1, wk​−1 zeros on every border and run valid mode cross-correlation with K rotated 180°.

Transposed Convolution 2D may be visualized as follows:

conv2D operation produces a shrunken filtered image, while conv2Dtranspose produces an expanded image.

1.1.1 Properties of Base Operations [P-1.1]

1. [Bilinearity of Base Operations]

Given K1​,K2​,K∈Rhk​×wk​, X1​,X2​,X∈Rhx​×wx​,

1. [Bilinearity of ⋆]

  1. (αK1​+βK2​)⋆X= α(K1​⋆X)+β(K2​⋆X)
  2. K⋆(αX1​+βX2​)= α(K⋆X1​)+β(K⋆X2​)

2. [Bilinearity of ⋆⊤]

  1. (αK1​+βK2​)⋆⊤X= α(K1​⋆⊤X)+β(K2​⋆⊤X)
  2. K⋆⊤(αX1​+βX2​)= α(K⋆⊤X1​)+β(K⋆⊤X2​)
Proof

1.1 [⋆ linearity in K] Let Y=(αK1​+βK2​)⋆X

Then, by Def. 1.1.1,

∴∴∴​Yi,j​=m,n∑​(α⋅K1m,n​+β⋅K2m,n​)⋅Xi+m,j+n​Yi,j​=m,n∑​α⋅K1m,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​+β⋅K2m,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​Yi,j​=α⋅m,n∑​K1m,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​+β⋅m,n∑​K2m,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​Y=α(K1​⋆X)+β(K2​⋆X)q.e.d​

1.2 [⋆ linearity in X] Let Y=K⋆(αX1​+βX2​)

Then, by Def. 1.1.1,

∴∴∴​Yi,j​=m,n∑​Km,n​⋅(α⋅X1i+m,j+n​+β⋅X2i+m,j+n​)Yi,j​=m,n∑​α⋅Km,n​⋅X1i+m,j+n​+β⋅Km,n​⋅X2i+m,j+n​Yi,j​=α⋅m,n∑​Km,n​⋅X1i+m,j+n​+β⋅m,n∑​Km,n​⋅X2i+m,j+n​Y=α(K⋆X1​)+β(K⋆X2​)q.e.d​

Proofs of 2.1 & 2.2 come about from Definition 1.1.2, where Y=K⋆⊤X =rot180(K)⋆ pad(X;hk​−1,wk​−1).

Both rotation and pad operator are linear in operands, which when coupled with P-1.1.1.1 proved above, yields the bilinearity of ⋆⊤.

By linear operator, T(α⋅x+β⋅y) =α⋅T(x)+β⋅T(y) is the definition used. q.e.d.

2. [Adjoint Identity]

Given K∈Rhk​×wk​, X∈Rhx​×wx​ and G∈Rhg​×wg​ such that

  • hg​=hx​−hk​+1
  • wg​=wx​−wk​+1

Define ⟨A,B⟩=tr(A⊤B), where A,B∈Rm×n. This is Frobenius inner product.

⟨K⋆X,G⟩=⟨X,K⋆⊤G⟩​

Proof

∴∴∴∴​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(K⋆X)i,j​→Definition of Frobenius inner product⟨K⋆X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(m,n=0∑hk​−1,wk​−1​Km,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​)→Def. 1.1.1, Cross-Correlation⟨K⋆X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​i,j=0∑hg​−1wg​−1​​Gi,j​⋅Km,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​i=mj=n​∑hg​+m−1wg​+n−1​​Gi−m,j−n​⋅Km,n​⋅Xi,j​Define Gi,jpad​={Gi,j​,0,​0≤i≤hg​−1,0≤j≤wg​−1otherwise​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​i,j=0∑hg​+hk​−2wg​+wk​−2​​Gi−m,j−npad​⋅Km,n​⋅Xi,j​​

The last two steps essentially add zero terms into the mix, since it is evident that the internal summation is being expanded by inserting more indices for which G will have undefined values.

The last two steps:

  1. Defining a Gi,jpad​ pads hk​−1 zeros on top and bottom borders, wk​−1 zeros on left and right borders, and indices now run from −hk​−1 to hk​+hg​−2 for rows and −wk​−1 to wk​+wg​−2 for columns.

  2. Continuing from step 1, to expand the summation, for any (i−m,j−n) outside index range of G, it will be zero, meaning Gi−m,j−npad​⋅Xi,j​ can be added without any consequences.

Hence,

∴​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​+hk​−2wg​+wk​−2​​Xi,j​m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅Gi−m,j−npad​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=tr(X⊤(K⋆⊤G))=⟨X,K⋆⊤G⟩​

q.e.d

3. [Swap Identity]

Given K∈Rhk​×wk​, X∈Rhx​×wx​ and G∈Rhg​×wg​ such that

  • hg​=hx​−hk​+1
  • wg​=wx​−wk​+1

⟨G,K⋆X⟩=⟨G⋆X,K⟩​

Proof

∴∴∴∴∴​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(K⋆X)i,j​→Definition of Frobenius inner product⟨K⋆X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(m,n=0∑hk​−1,wk​−1​Km,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​)→Def. 1.1.1, Cross-Correlation⟨K⋆X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​i,j=0∑hg​−1wg​−1​​Gi,j​⋅Km,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅i,j=0∑hg​−1wg​−1​​Gi,j​⋅Xi+m,j+n​⟨K⋆X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅(G⋆X)m,n​→Def. 1.1.1, cross-correlation⟨K⋆X,G⟩=⟨K,G⋆X⟩​

q.e.d

These two properties will be invaluable for deriving the backprop with ease.

In fact, the existence of transposed convolution comes about from the second property and the idea of how it is derived will be useful in deriving the adjoint of the strided CNN layers.

1.2 Conv2D and Conv2DTranspose

There are two layers that come about from this, one used to create smaller images and one for bigger images, the convolution (conv2D) & transposed convolution (conv2Dtranspose) layer. These can collectively be called the convolution layers.

Definition 1.2 [Forward Pass of convolution layers]

1. [Convolution Layer (conv2D)]
The convolution layer (conv2D) takes in a channeled image, X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, has kernels arranged in a 4D tensor: K∈ Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in a 3D tensor B∈ Rco​×ho​×wo​. The output space Y=Rco​×ho​×wo​ :

​Yi​∈Rho​×wo​,i=0,1,⋯co​−1, where ho​=hi​−hk​+1,wo​=wi​−wk​+1​Y0​=j=0∑ci​−1​K0,j​⋆Xj​+B0​Y1​=j=0∑ci​−1​K1,j​⋆Xj​+B1​⋮Yco​−1​=j=0∑ci​−1​Kc0​−1,j​⋆Xj​+Bco​−1​​​

The last set of equations can be compactly written as:

​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆Xj​+Bi​∈Rho​×wo​i=0,1,⋯co​−1​​

2. [Transposed Convolution Layer (Conv2DTranspose)]
The transposed convolution layer takes in a channeled image, X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, has kernels arranged in a 4D tensor K∈ Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in a 3D tensor B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​. The output space Y=Rco​×ho​×wo​ :

​Yi​∈Rho​×wo​,i=0,1,⋯co​−1, where ho​=hi​+hk​−1,wo​=wi​+wk​−1​Y0​=j=0∑ci​−1​K0,j​⋆TXj​+B0​Y1​=j=0∑ci​−1​K1,j​⋆TXj​+B1​⋮Yco​−1​=j=0∑ci​−1​Kco​−1,j​⋆TXj​+Bco​−1​​​

Compactly:

​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆TXj​+Bi​∈Rho​×wo​i=0,1,⋯co​−1​​

PyTorch indexes the filters abit differently, but for consistency, the indexing is used like so over here.

NOTE

1. Notice that this can be written almost like a linear layer.

​Y0​Y1​⋮Yco​−1​​​=​K0,0​K1,0​⋮Kco​−1,0​​K0,1​K1,1​⋮Kco​−1,1​​⋯⋯⋱⋯​K0,ci​−1​K1,ci​−1​⋮Kco​−1,ci​−1​​​⋆​X0​X1​⋮Xci​−1​​​⊕​B0​B1​⋮Bco​−1​​​

In the matrix multiplication, the multiplication is replaced by cross-correlation, the addition is elementwise. All the elements in the matrices and vectors are real matrices.

2. Same trick can be played with transposed convolution

​Y0​Y1​⋮Yco​−1​​​=​K0,0​K1,0​⋮Kco​−1,0​​K0,1​K1,1​⋮Kco​−1,1​​⋯⋯⋱⋯​K0,ci​−1​K1,ci​−1​⋮Kco​−1,ci​−1​​​⋆⊤​X0​X1​⋮Xci​−1​​​⊕​B0​B1​⋮Bco​−1​​​

Where multiplication is replaced with the transposed convolution operation, and addition as usual is elementwise, with elements of matrices and vectors being real matrices.

These matmul perspectives are taken from this video, credits where they’re due.

3. The thing that every lecture on CNN will mention at some point: convolution layer (conv2D) is not convolution, it is cross correlation. But transposed convolution is actual convolution.

1.3 Backward Pass

Theorem 1.1 [Gradients in Base Operations]

1. Let X∈Rhi​×wi​ and K∈Rhk​×wk​, with Y=K⋆X∈Rho​×wo​, dimensions calculated as per Definition 1.1.1. Then, given δY​∈Rho​×wo​, which is δY​≡∂Y∂l​,

​δK​≡∂K∂l​=δY​⋆XδX​≡∂X∂l​=K⋆⊤δY​​​

2. Let X∈Rhi​×wi​ and K∈Rhk​×wk​, with Y=K⋆⊤X∈Rho​×wo​, dimensions calculated as per Definition 1.1.2. Then, given δY​∈Rho​×wo​, which is δY​≡∂Y∂l​,

​δK​≡∂K∂l​=X⋆δY​δX​≡∂X∂l​=K⋆δY​​​

Proof

1. Given Y=K⋆X, with each matrix having the appropriate dimensions,

∴∴∴​dY=K⋆dX+dK⋆Xdl=⟨δY​,dY⟩=⟨δY​,K⋆dX+dK⋆X⟩dl=⟨δY​,K⋆dX⟩+⟨δY​,dK⋆X⟩dl=⟨K⋆⊤δY​,dX⟩→P-1.1.2, Adjoint Identity+⟨δY​⋆X,dK⟩→P-1.1.3, Swap Identitydl=⟨δX​,dX⟩+⟨δK​,dK⟩→Total Derivative Theorem​

This gives us:

​δX​=K⋆⊤δY​δK​=δY​⋆X​​

q.e.d

2. Given Y=K⋆⊤X, with each matrix having the appropriate dimensions,

∴∴∴​dY=K⋆⊤dX+dK⋆⊤Xdl=⟨δY​,dY⟩=⟨δY​,K⋆⊤dX⟩+⟨δY​,dK⋆⊤X⟩dl=⟨dX,K⋆δY​⟩+⟨dK⋆δY​,X⟩→P-1.1.2, P-1.1.3dl=⟨dX,K⋆δY​⟩+⟨dK,X⋆δY​⟩​

Hence, by total derivative theorem,

​δK​=X⋆δY​δX​=K⋆δY​​​

q.e.d

Theorem 1.2 [Conv2D & Conv2Dtranspose backpass]

1. Given Conv2D layer, with input expected to be in Rci​×hi​×wi​, and output expected to be in Rco​×ho​×wo​, with kernels in Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in Rco​×ho​×wo​, given the output gradient δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​

​δKi,j​=δY,i​⋆Xj​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆⊤δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​​

Very similar to linear layer in some sense.

2. Given Conv2Dtranpose layer, with input expected to be in Rci​×hi​×wi​, and output expected to be in Rco​×ho​×wo​, with kernels in Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in Rco​×ho​×wo​, given the output gradient δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​

​δKi,j​=Xj​⋆δY,i​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​​

Proof

1. The forward pass for conv2D can be compactly written as:

∴∴∴∴∴​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆Xj​+Bi​0≤i≤co​−1→Def. 1.1.1, conv2D forwarddYi​=j∑​(dKi,j​⋆Xj​+Ki,j​⋆dXj​)+dBi​dl=i∑​tr(δY,i⊤​⋅dYi​)→total derivitive theoremdl=i,j∑​⟨δY,i​,dKi,j​⋆Xj​⟩+⟨δY,i​,Ki,j​⋆dXj​⟩+i∑​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩dl=i,j∑​⟨δY,i​⋆Xj​,dKi,j​⟩+⟨Ki,j​⋆⊤δY,i​,dXj​⟩+i∑​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩→From Theorem 1.1.1dl=i,j∑​⟨δY,i​⋆Xj​,dKi,j​⟩+j∑​⟨i∑​Ki,j​⋆⊤δY,i​,dXj​⟩+i∑​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩→Linearity of inner product​

Using total derivitive theorem, the gradients come out as:

​δKi,j​=δY,i​⋆Xj​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆⊤δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​​

2. The forward pass for conv2Dtranspose is:

∴∴∴∴∴​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆⊤Xj​+Bi​0≤i≤co​−1→Def. 1.1.1, conv2Dtranspose forwarddYi​=j∑​(dKi,j​⋆⊤Xj​+Ki,j​⋆⊤dXj​)+dBi​dl=i∑​tr(δY,i⊤​⋅dYi​)→total derivitive theoremdl=i,j∑​⟨δY,i​,dKi,j​⋆⊤Xj​⟩+⟨δY,i​,Ki,j​⋆⊤dXj​⟩+i∑​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩dl=i,j∑​⟨Xj​⋆δY,i​,dKi,j​⟩+⟨Ki,j​⋆δY,i​,dXj​⟩+i∑​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩→From Theorem 1.1.2dl=i,j∑​⟨Xj​⋆δY,i​,dKi,j​⟩+j∑​⟨i∑​Ki,j​⋆δY,i​,dXj​⟩+i∑​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩→Linearity of inner product​

Hence, total derivitive theorem gives you:

​δKi,j​=Xj​⋆δY,i​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​​

q.e.d

1.4 Algorithms for single input

1.4.1 Forward Pass

Algorithm 1.1 [conv2D Single Input Forward Pass (SIFP)]

Input

  • X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2D layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​

Output

  • Y∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, the output of the conv2D forward pass.

Algorithm

  1. for i=0 to co​−1 do
    1. Yi​←Bi​
    2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. Yi​←Yi​+Ki,j​⋆Xj​
    3. end for
  2. end for
  3. return Y

Algorithm 1.2 [conv2Dtranspose Single Input Forward Pass (SIFP)]

Input

  • X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2Dtranspose layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​

Output

  • Y∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, output of the conv2Dtranspose forward pass.

Algorithm

  1. for i=0 to co​−1 do
    1. Yi​←Bi​
    2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. Yi​←Yi​+Ki,j​⋆⊤Xj​
    3. end for
  2. end for
  3. return Y

1.4.2 Backward Pass

Algorithm 1.3 [conv2D Single Input Backward Pass (SIBP)]

Input

  • δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, output gradient.
  • [Cached] X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2D layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​

Output

  • δK​,δB​,δX​, parameter and input gradients of the network.

Algorithm

  1. δB​←δY​ Theorem 1.2.1, bias gradient
  2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do input gradients
    1. δX,j​←0hi​×wi​​
    2. for i=0 to co​−1 do
      1. δX,j​←δX,j​+Ki,j​⋆⊤δY,i​ Theorem 1.2.1
    3. end for
  3. end for
  4. for i=0 to co​−1 do kernel gradients
    1. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. δK,i,j​←δY,i​⋆Xj​ Theorem 1.2.1
    2. end for
  5. end for
  6. return δK​,δB​,δX​

Algorithm 1.4 [conv2Dtranspose Single Input Backward Pass (SIBP)]

Input

  • δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, output gradient.
  • [Cached] X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2Dtranspose layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​

Output

  • δK​,δB​,δX​, parameter and input gradients of the network.

Algorithm

  1. δB​←δY​ Theorem 1.2.2, bias gradient
  2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do input gradients
    1. δX,j​←0hi​×wi​​
    2. for i=0 to co​−1 do
      1. δX,j​←δX,j​+Ki,j​⋆δY,i​ Theorem 1.2.2
    3. end for
  3. end for
  4. for i=0 to co​−1 do kernel gradients
    1. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. δK,i,j​←Xj​⋆δY,i​ Theorem 1.2.2
    2. end for
  5. end for
  6. return δK​,δB​,δX​

2. Strided CNN

One of the thing being done uptil now, is: the stride of the sliding window in the forward pass is assumed to be 1 in both directions.

What is the case when strides are (sr​,sc​) which is: sr​ stride for row and sc​ stride in columns? How does the adjoint operator work for that?

These are the questions that are answered in this section.

2.1 Base Strided Operations

Definition 2.1 [Strided Base Ops]

1. [Strided Cross-Correlation]

Given a matrix X∈Rhx​×wx​ and a kernel K∈Rhk​×wk​, then given strides (r,s) in the row and column axis for the sliding window, the strided cross correlation is a matrix Y∈Rhy​×wy​ where:

  • hy​=⌊rhx​−hk​​⌋+1
  • wy​=⌊swx​−wk​​⌋+1

and the elements of Y are calculated as follows:

Yi,j​=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​Xir+m,js+n​​

in short denoted as: Y=K⋆(r,s)​X

2. [Strided Transposed Convolution]

Given a matrix X∈Rhx​×wx​ and a kernel K∈Rhk​×wk​, the strided transposed convolution with upsample ratios (r,s) is a matrix Y∈Rhy​×wy​=K⋆(r,s)⊤​X :

  • hy​=(hx​−1)r+hk​
  • wy​=(wx​−1)s+wk​

K⋆(r,s)⊤​X=K⋆⊤(X↑(r,s))≡K⋆⊤U(X;r,s)​​

Where ↑ and U denote the upsample operator. It adds r−1 zeros between adjacent cols and s−1 zeros between elements of adjacent rows.

X↑(r,s)={Xi/r,j/s​0​i,j≡0(mod r,s)otherwise​

The shape of which will be: ((hx​−1)r+1,(wx​−1)s+1). This is the adjoint operation of the strided cross-corr.

2.1.1 Properties of Strided Base Ops [P-2.1]

1. [Bilinearity of Base Operations]

Given K1​,K2​∈Rhk​×wk​, X1​,X2​∈Rhx​×wx​,

1. [Bilinearity of ⋆(r,s)​]

  1. (αK1​+βK2​)⋆(r,s)​X= α(K1​⋆(r,s)​X)+β(K2​⋆(r,s)​X)
  2. K⋆(r,s)​(αX1​+βX2​)= α(K⋆(r,s)​X1​)+β(K⋆(r,s)​X2​)

2. [Bilinearity of ⋆(r,s)⊤​]

  1. (αK1​+βK2​)⋆(r,s)⊤​X= α(K1​⋆(r,s)⊤​X)+β(K2​⋆(r,s)⊤​X)
  2. K⋆(r,s)⊤​(αX1​+βX2​)= α(K⋆(r,s)⊤​X1​)+β(K⋆(r,s)⊤​X2​)
Proof

1.1 [⋆(r,s)​ linearity in K]
Let Y=(αK1​+βK2​)⋆(r,s)​X

Then, by Def. 2.1.1,

∴∴∴​Yi,j​=m,n∑​(α⋅K1m,n​+β⋅K2m,n​)⋅Xir+m,js+n​Yi,j​=m,n∑​α⋅K1m,n​⋅Xir+m,js+n​+β⋅K2m,n​⋅Xir+m,js+n​Yi,j​=α⋅m,n∑​K1m,n​⋅Xir+m,js+n​+β⋅m,n∑​K2m,n​⋅Xir+m,js+n​Y=α(K1​⋆(r,s)​X)+β(K2​⋆(r,s)​X)q.e.d​

1.2 [⋆(r,s)​ linearity in X]
Let Y=K⋆(r,s)​(αX1​+βX2​)

Then, by Def. 2.1.1,

∴∴∴​Yi,j​=m,n∑​Km,n​⋅(α⋅X1ir+m,js+n​+β⋅X2ir+m,js+n​)Yi,j​=m,n∑​α⋅Km,n​⋅X1ir+m,js+n​+β⋅Km,n​⋅X2ir+m,js+n​Yi,j​=α⋅m,n∑​Km,n​⋅X1ir+m,js+n​+β⋅m,n∑​Km,n​⋅X2ir+m,js+n​Y=α(K⋆(r,s)​X1​)+β(K⋆(r,s)​X2​)q.e.d​

Proofs of 2.1 & 2.2 come about from Definition 2.1.2, where Y=K⋆(r,s)⊤​X =K⋆⊤U(X;r,s).

The upsample operator is linear in X, which when coupled with P-1.1.1, yields the bilinearity of ⋆(r,s)⊤​.

q.e.d.

2. [Adjoint Identity (Strided)]

Given K∈Rhk​×wk​, X∈Rhx​×wx​, strides r,s∈Z+ and G∈Rhg​×wg​ such that

  • hg​=⌊rhx​−hk​​⌋+1
  • wg​=⌊swx​−wk​​⌋+1

Define the dilation operator, for G∈Rhg​×wg​:

(G↑(r,s))u,v​={Gu/r,v/s​,0,​u≡0 (mod r), v≡0 (mod s)0≤u/r≤hg​−1, 0≤v/s≤wg​−1​otherwise​

and K⋆(r,s)T​G:=K⋆⊤(G↑(r,s)).

⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=⟨X,K⋆(r,s)⊤​G⟩​

Proof

∴∴∴∴​⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(K⋆r,s​X)i,j​→Definition of Frobenius inner product⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(m,n=0∑hk​−1,wk​−1​Km,n​⋅Xri+m,sj+n​)→Def. Strided Cross-Correlation⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​i,j=0∑hg​−1wg​−1​​Gi,j​⋅Km,n​⋅Xri+m,sj+n​Substitute p=ri+m, q=sj+n, valid only whenp≡m (mod r), q≡n (mod s)⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​p≡m(r)q≡n(s)​∑​G(p−m)/r,(q−n)/s​⋅Km,n​⋅Xp,q​By definition of ↑(r,s), G(p−m)/r,(q−n)/s​=(G↑(r,s))p−m,q−n​whenever the congruence and range conditions hold,and (G↑(r,s))p−m,q−n​=0 otherwise.⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​p,q=0∑hx​−1wx​−1​​(G↑(r,s))p−m,q−n​⋅Km,n​⋅Xp,q​​

The last step extends the sum over p,q to the full domain of X: for any (p,q) outside the valid congruence classes or range, (G↑(r,s))p−m,q−n​=0 by definition, so these extra terms contribute nothing, exactly as the zero-padding argument did in the unstrided case — the only difference is that the “gaps” being filled with zero here are interspersed (dilation) rather than only at the border (padding).

Hence,

∴​⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=p,q=0∑hx​−1wx​−1​​Xp,q​m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅(G↑(r,s))p−m,q−n​⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=tr(X⊤(K⋆⊤(G↑(r,s))))=⟨X,K⋆(r,s)⊤​G⟩​

q.e.d

This is where the ajoint operator comes from. The strided transposed convolution does not come about magically. It is the adjoint operator for a reason.

For more general cases, this property can be used to serve as the definition of adjoint operator.

3. [Swap Identity (Strided)]

Given K∈Rhk​×wk​, X∈Rhx​×wx​, strides r,s∈Z+ and G∈Rhg​×wg​ such that

  • hg​=⌊rhx​−hk​​⌋+1
  • wg​=⌊swx​−wk​​⌋+1

⟨G,K⋆(r,s)​X⟩=⟨(G↑(r,s))⋆X,K⟩​

Proof

∴∴∴∴∴∴​⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(K⋆(r,s)​X)i,j​→Definition of Frobenius inner product⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=i,j=0∑hg​−1,wg​−1​Gi,j​⋅(m,n=0∑hk​−1,wk​−1​Km,n​⋅Xri+m,sj+n​)→Def. Strided Cross-Correlation⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​i,j=0∑hg​−1wg​−1​​Gi,j​⋅Km,n​⋅Xri+m,sj+n​⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅i,j=0∑hg​−1wg​−1​​Gi,j​⋅Xri+m,sj+n​Substitute p=ri, q=sj, so Gi,j​=(G↑(r,s))p,q​and Xri+m,sj+n​=Xp+m,q+n​, with (G↑(r,s))p,q​=0for all p,q not a multiple of r,s respectively⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅p,q=0∑r(hg​−1)s(wg​−1)​​(G↑(r,s))p,q​⋅Xp+m,q+n​⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=m,n=0∑hk​−1wk​−1​​Km,n​⋅((G↑(r,s))⋆X)m,n​→Def. 1.1.1, cross-correlation⟨K⋆(r,s)​X,G⟩=⟨K,(G↑(r,s))⋆X⟩​

q.e.d

2.2 Strided conv2D and conv2Dtranspose

Definition 2.2 [strided conv2D & conv2Dtranspose layer]

1. [Strided Convolution Layer (conv2D)]
The convolution layer (conv2D) takes in a channeled image, X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, has kernels arranged in a 4D tensor: K∈ Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in a 3D tensor B∈ Rco​×ho​×wo​. The stride is fixed to (r,s) and the output space is Y=Rco​×ho​×wo​ :

​Yi​∈Rho​×wo​,i=0,1,⋯co​−1, where ho​=⌊rhi​−hk​​⌋+1,wo​=⌊swi​−wk​​⌋+1​Y0​=j=0∑ci​−1​K0,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​+B0​Y1​=j=0∑ci​−1​K1,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​+B1​⋮Yco​−1​=j=0∑ci​−1​Kc0​−1,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​+Bco​−1​​​

The last set of equations can be compactly written as:

​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​+Bi​∈Rho​×wo​i=0,1,⋯co​−1​​

2. [Strided Transposed Convolution Layer (Conv2DTranspose)]
The transposed convolution layer takes in a channeled image, X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, has kernels arranged in a 4D tensor K∈ Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in a 3D tensor B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​. The stride (upsample ratio) is fixed to (r,s) and the output space Y=Rco​×ho​×wo​ :

​Yi​∈Rho​×wo​,i=0,1,⋯co​−1, where ho​=(hi​−1)r+hk​,wo​=(wi​−1)s+wk​​Y0​=j=0∑ci​−1​K0,j​⋆(r,s)T​Xj​+B0​Y1​=j=0∑ci​−1​K1,j​⋆(r,s)T​Xj​+B1​⋮Yco​−1​=j=0∑ci​−1​Kco​−1,j​⋆(r,s)T​Xj​+Bco​−1​​​

Compactly:

​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)T​Xj​+Bi​∈Rho​×wo​i=0,1,⋯co​−1​​

2.3 Backward Pass

This section will deal with the backward pass of the two layers.

Theorem 2.1 [strided backward operations]

1. Let X∈Rhi​×wi​ and K∈Rhk​×wk​, with Y=K⋆(r,s)​X∈Rho​×wo​, dimensions calculated as per Definition 2.1.1. Then, given the strides of the layer: (r,s), and given δY​∈Rho​×wo​, which is δY​≡∂Y∂l​,

​δK​≡∂K∂l​=U(δY​;r,s)⋆XδX​≡∂X∂l​=K⋆(r,s)⊤​δY​​​

2. Let X∈Rhi​×wi​ and K∈Rhk​×wk​, with Y=K⋆(r,s)⊤​X∈Rho​×wo​, dimensions calculated as per Definition 2.1.2. Then, given δY​∈Rho​×wo​, which is δY​≡∂Y∂l​,

​δK​≡∂K∂l​=U(X;r,s)⋆δY​δX​≡∂X∂l​=K⋆(r,s)​δY​​​

Proof

1. Y=K⋆(r,s)​X, hence :

∴∴∴​dY=dK⋆(r,s)​X+K⋆(r,s)​dXtr(δY⊤​⋅dY)=⟨δY​,dK⋆(r,s)​X⟩+⟨δY​,K⋆(r,s)​dX⟩→Linearity of inner producttr(δY⊤​⋅dY)=⟨U(δY​;r,s)⋆X,dK⟩→P-2.1.3, Swap Identity+⟨K⋆(r,s)⊤​δY​,dX⟩→P-2.1.2, Adjoint Identity​δX​=K⋆(r,s)⊤​δY​δK​=U(δY​;r,s)⋆X​→Total Derivitive Thm​

2. Y=K⋆(r,s)⊤​X. Hence :

∴∴∴∴​dY=dK⋆(r,s)⊤​X+K⋆(r,s)⊤​dXtr(δY⊤​⋅dY)=⟨δY​,dK⋆(r,s)⊤​X⟩+⟨δY​,K⋆(r,s)⊤​dX⟩→Linearity of inner producttr(δY⊤​⋅dY)=⟨X,dK⋆(r,s)​δY​⟩+⟨K⋆(r,s)​δY​,dX⟩→P-2.1.2, Adjoint Identitytr(δY⊤​⋅dY)=⟨U(X;r,s)⋆δY​,dK⟩+⟨K⋆(r,s)​δY​,dX⟩→P-2.1.3, Swap Identity​δX​=K⋆(r,s)​δY​δK​=U(X;r,s)⋆δY​​→Total Derivitive Thm​

q.e.d

Theorem 2.2 [conv2D & conv2Dtranposed strided backprop]

1. Given Conv2D layer, with input expected to be in Rci​×hi​×wi​, and output expected to be in Rco​×ho​×wo​, with kernels in Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in Rco​×ho​×wo​, given the output gradient δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, and the stride is: (r,s)

​δKi,j​=U(δY,i​;r,s)⋆Xj​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​​

2. Given Conv2Dtranpose layer, with input expected to be in Rci​×hi​×wi​, and output expected to be in Rco​×ho​×wo​, with kernels in Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​ and biases in Rco​×ho​×wo​, given the output gradient δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​ with upsample scales : (r,s)

​δKi,j​=U(Xj​;r,s)⋆δY,i​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​​

Proof

1. By Definition 2.2.1, the forward pass for conv2D strided version is:

​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​+Bi​∈Rho​×wo​i=0,1,⋯co​−1​

Based on this:

​dYi​=j=0∑ci​−1​dKi,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​+j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​dXj​+dBi​i=0,1,⋯co​−1dl=i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dYi​⟩→Total Derivitive Theorem​​dl=i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨δY,i​,dKi,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​⟩+i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨δY,i​,Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​dXj​⟩+i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩dl=P-2.1.3, Swap Identityi,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨U(δY,i​;r,s)⋆Xj​,dKi,j​⟩​​+P-2.1.2, Adjoint Identityi,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​δY,i​,dXj​⟩​​+i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩dl=i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨U(δY,i​;r,s)⋆Xj​,dKi,j​⟩+j=0∑ci​−1​⟨i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​δY,i​,dXj​⟩+⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩​

This gives the actual gradients:

​δKi,j​=U(δY,i​;r,s)⋆Xj​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​→Total Derivitive Thm

2. By Definition 2.2.2, the forward pass for conv2Dtranspose strided version is:

​Yi​=j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​Xj​+Bi​∈Rho​×wo​i=0,1,⋯co​−1​

Based on this:

​dYi​=j=0∑ci​−1​dKi,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​Xj​+j=0∑ci​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​dXj​+dBi​i=0,1,⋯co​−1dl=i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dYi​⟩→Total Derivitive Theorem​​dl=i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨δY,i​,dKi,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​Xj​⟩+i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨δY,i​,Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​dXj​⟩+i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩dl=i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨Xj​,dKij​⋆(r,s)​δY,i​⟩+i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​δY,i​,dXj​⟩+i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩→P-2.1.2, Adjoint Identitydl=i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨U(Xj​;r,s)⋆δY,i​,dKij​⟩+i,j=0∑co​−1ci​−1​​⟨Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​δY,i​,dXj​⟩+i=0∑co​−1​⟨δY,i​,dBi​⟩→P-2.1.3, Swap Identity​

This gives the actual gradients:

​δKi,j​=U(Xj​;r,s)⋆δY,i​​0≤i≤co​−10≤j≤ci​−1​δB​=δY​δX,j​=i=0∑co​−1​Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​δY,i​0≤j≤ci​−1​→Total Derivitive Thm

q.e.d

2.4 Algorithms for Strided Case

2.4.1 Forward Pass

Algorithm 2.1 [conv2D strided SIFP]

Input

  • X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2D layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​
    • (r,s) the strides

Output

  • Y∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, the output of the conv2D strided forward pass

Algorithm

  1. for i=0 to co​−1 do
    1. Yi​←Bi​
    2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. Yi​←Yi​+Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​Xj​
    3. end for
  2. end for
  3. return Y

Algorithm 2.2 [conv2Dtranspose strided SIFP]

Input

  • X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2Dtranspose layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​
    • (r,s) the upsample ratios

Output

  • Y∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, output of the conv2Dtranspose forward pass.

Algorithm

  1. for i=0 to co​−1 do
    1. Yi​←Bi​
    2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. Yi​←Yi​+Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​Xj​
    3. end for
  2. end for
  3. return Y

2.4.2 Backward Pass

Algorithm 2.3 [conv2D strided SIBP]

Input

  • δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, output gradient.
  • [Cached] X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2D layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​
  • (r,s) the strides (decimation ratios)

Output

  • δK​,δB​,δX​, parameter and input gradients of the network.

Algorithm

  1. δB​←δY​ Theorem 2.2.1, bias gradient
  2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do input gradients
    1. δX,j​←0hi​×wi​​
    2. for i=0 to co​−1 do
      1. δX,j​←δX,j​+Ki,j​⋆(r,s)⊤​δY,i​ Theorem 2.2.1
    3. end for
  3. end for
  4. for i=0 to co​−1 do kernel gradients
    1. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. δK,i,j​←U(δY,i​;r,s)⋆Xj​ Theorem 2.2.1
    2. end for
  5. end for
  6. return δK​,δB​,δX​

Algorithm 2.4 [conv2Dtranspose Strided SIBP]

Input

  • δY​∈Rco​×ho​×wo​, output gradient.
  • [Cached] X∈Rci​×hi​×wi​, the input channeled image.
  • conv2Dtranspose layer parameters
    • K∈Rco​×ci​×hk​×wk​
    • B∈Rco​×ho​×wo​
  • (r,s) upsample ratios

Output

  • δK​,δB​,δX​, parameter and input gradients of the network.

Algorithm

  1. δB​←δY​ Theorem 2.2.2, bias gradient
  2. for j=0 to ci​−1 do input gradients
    1. δX,j​←0hi​×wi​​
    2. for i=0 to co​−1 do
      1. δX,j​←δX,j​+Ki,j​⋆(r,s)​δY,i​ Theorem 2.2.2
    3. end for
  3. end for
  4. for i=0 to co​−1 do kernel gradients
    1. for j=0 to ci​−1 do
      1. δK,i,j​←U(Xj​;r,s)⋆δY,i​ Theorem 2.2.2
    2. end for
  5. end for
  6. return δK​,δB​,δX​

3. Batching in CNNs

In MLP chapter, already established how to do batched backpropagation.

​L(θ;D)=N1​i=0∑N−1​l(xi​;yi​,θ)∇θ​L(θ;D)=N1​i=0∑N−1​∇θ​l(xi​;yi​,θ)∇θ​L(θ;D)=sum​−−−​∇θ​l(xi​;y0​,θ)⊤∇θ​l(xi​;y1​,θ)⊤⋮∇θ​l(xi​;yN−1​,θ)⊤​−−−​​​

Each row in the above matrix is a single backpass. The crucial part in CNN is efficient implementation of the base operations, since all the backprop ops contain these operations recurringly.

KEY TRICK

Cross-Correlation and Transposed Convolution are both linear in operands [P-1.1.1, P-2.1.1], meaning they can be represented as matrix multiplications. This is a linear algebra thing, but the point is that matmul is much more faster and hardware friendly than naive implementations of cross-corr. and transposed conv.

This will then allow us to use the techniques developed in MLP chapter and write everything in terms of Matmul ops.

3.1 im2col and col2im

To convert Y=K⋆X into matrix multiplications, the main function is: im2col. The key idea behind it is:

  1. vectorize/flatten the kernels K into a vector of size hk​⋅wk​≡nk​, hence vec(K)∈Rnk​.
  2. Yi,j​=∑m,n​Km,n​⋅Xi+m,j+n​ =vec(K)⊤ vec(Xi:i+hk​,j:j+wk​​)
  3. Hence, create Xcol​∈Rnk​×ny​ where ny​=hy​⋅wy​ and each col in Xc​ol is a vectoried patch.
  4. vec(Y)=Xcol⊤​vec(K) is the final operation. So, given the metadata about shapes of all the matrices, the result can be reshaped appropriately.
